$comment: Species are the unit of observation. Operational taxa in taxa.json are DERIVED from these — a clade's presence, division and attachment consensus are computed from its species, never authored. See docs/SCHEMA.md.

species.note: Devonian stem tetrapod, and the best-described humerus in the column — Coates (1996) names an attachment for most of its processes. Not a terrestrial animal: the reconstructions bear on aquatic limb-substrate interaction, not on support.
Hudson et al.'s functional anatomy, fore- and hindlimb.
One of the four animals Haas (1973) marks 'Haas, this chapter' in his own list of forms studied, and the agamid his original figures 34, 35, 38 and 40 are drawn from.
Meers's main dissection.
Abdala & Diogo's caudate exemplar.
Terrestrial, in Omura et al.'s habitat series.

Ground lizards. Teiid, paired with Cnemidophorus in Fisher & Tanner's work. **Genus-level record**: the sources name the genus and not always a species, so rows land here rather than on a binomial nobody stated.
Westphal et al. compare several worm-lizard genera at different degrees of limb reduction rather than dissecting one; rows citing it are a within-clade generalisation.
Aquatic, elongate.

American eel. Springer & Johnson (2015) describe its gill-arch musculature from four specimens, correcting two readings in Smith & Johnson (2004). The familiar anguillid against Protanguilla, which is hypothesised to be the sister group of all other eels — so the pair shows what an eel retained and what one lost.
Anoles. Arboreal dactyloids with adhesive toepads. **Genus-level record**: the sources name the genus and not always a species, so rows land here rather than on a binomial nobody stated.
Jayaram, Dhanze & Singh (1983), one of three ariid catfishes whose cranial muscles they compare. Its adductor mandibulae has six elements and its intramandibularis is the best developed of the three.
Jayaram, Dhanze & Singh (1983). The species their summary says has five adductor mandibulae elements — though their own descriptions give it six; see the reading note.
Declared partly out of scope; cranial only.
Jayaram, Dhanze & Singh (1983). Resembles A. arius in most of the cranial musculature, differing chiefly in how tendinous several origins are.

Desert grassland whiptail (Teiidae). Molnar et al. (2017) use it as the non-arboreal comparative outgroup for chameleon limb myology; it has neither syndactyly nor zygodactyly. A teiid, so a relatively distant reference — the closest non-arboreal sister group to Chamaeleonidae would be an agamid, which they did not dissect.

Philippine flat-headed frog, a bombinatorid. Prikryl et al. (2009) dissected it for its phylogenetically basal position; they print the specific epithet as *busagensis*. Its trunk musculature is the most modified of their nine frogs — the transversus reaches onto the dorsum.
Cunningham's *Bathyergus capensis*, from the Challenger Commission. With the Cape mouse it is his clearest case of a foot in which the flexores breves are the only intrinsic muscles left.
Oriental fire-bellied toad. One of Prikryl et al.'s (2009) nine frogs, and the closest comparison to their Discoglossus baseline — both discoglossoid-grade.
The second term of Cunningham's horse–ox–sheep series on the suspensory ligament. The ox's holds more muscle than the horse's and is built from two short flexors rather than one.

The three-toed sloth, and the most extreme foot in Cunningham's survey: the proximal phalanges fuse to the metatarsal heads early in life, abolishing the metatarsophalangeal joint, and **not a vestige of an intrinsic muscle remains in the sole**. Only the dorsal interossei survive, kept on for a secondary action they share with the extensor apparatus.
Spotted toad (now usually Rhaebo guttatus). One of Prikryl et al.'s (2009) nine frogs, sampled as a bufonid walker rather than a jumper.
Abdala & Diogo's crocodylian exemplar.
Pereyra et al.'s crural and pedal myology.
Holocephalan, against the elasmobranch exemplars.
Schilling's mammal for epaxial activity during locomotion (m. longissimus thoracis et lumborum, 6th lumbar vertebra). A large quadruped, and not a proxy for Theria.
Dissected by Walker (1973), Cheloniidae — **pelvic limb only**. A marine turtle whose limb is a flipper.
A putrid specimen carefully dissected. Its interest is that most of what is missing is present as fibrous bands, as in the armadillo.

Not an animal. Prikryl et al. (2009) dissected three caudates — Necturus (3 specimens), Ambystoma (3) and one adult Salamandra salamandra — as an outgroup baseline for the anuran pelvis, and describe the result as a caudate pattern rather than three descriptions: their text opens 'In all caudates', and each muscle carries figure references to all three animals at once. Their stated reasoning is that the neotenic caudates are the best available proxy for the aquatic temnospondyl ancestors of frogs. Where they do separate the animals, the row says so.
Widrig et al.'s diceCT specimen (USNM 666527), with correlates read off USNM 345619 and 646637.
Dissected by Walker (1973), Chelidae. His second pleurodire.
Terrestrial, in Pereyra et al.'s histological series.
Hattori & Tsuihiji's only turtle, and the sole chelonian behind their pedal homologies. A cryptodire, so it says nothing about the pleurodire condition.
Werneburg & Maier's cryptodire developmental series, read against the pleurodire Emydura subglobosa. An emydid like Trachemys, which is why it stands where the turtle column already sits.
Whiptails. Teiid, paired with Ameiva. **Genus-level record**: the sources name the genus and not always a species, so rows land here rather than on a binomial nobody stated.

Jones et al.'s CT specimen, an adult of 242 g. Their own caution is worth carrying: Columba livia includes some 350 breeds, so 'the pigeon' is a wide target, and their descriptions differ in places from earlier accounts of the same species.

Longfin African conger. Springer & Johnson (2015) use it as the reference eel against which Anguilla and Synaphobranchus are read; its dorsal gill-arch muscles are Smith & Johnson's (2004) descriptions, reported rather than redescribed.

Collared lizards. Bipedal runners; Davis (1934) and Robison & Tanner (1962) disagree on the number of bellies. **Genus-level record**: the sources name the genus and not always a species, so rows land here rather than on a binomial nobody stated.

Johnston (2014) figures the lizard jaw adductors on this animal, chosen because the absence of a ventral temporal arch makes the layering legible. Not a general lizard: he takes Sphenodon, not an iguanid, as the plesiomorphic lepidosaur condition.
Semi-aquatic.

The Challenger brought three, and Cunningham chose others for the full dissection — but he examined its hand alongside the thylacine's, and its pes is one of the feet in the comparative survey, so it enters the dataset through the extremities rather than through a whole-animal description.
Desert iguana. The iguanian in Schilling's axial figures. **Genus-level record**: the sources name the genus and not always a species, so rows land here rather than on a binomial nobody stated.
Prikryl et al.'s main dissection.

Cunningham's *Elephas indicus* — the feet of a foetal specimen from the Edinburgh museum, checked against Miall & Greenwood. Its intrinsic muscles are reduced for the reason he gives: digits encased in tough integument and a thick plantar cushion have nowhere to be separated or approximated to.

Werneburg's own animal — a subadult micro-CT'd specimen, PIMUZ labNo. 2009.37. A pleurodire, and proposed in the literature as a pleurodiran model species. Present here with no rows yet: separating what Werneburg observed in Emydura from what he compiled across Testudines needs the body of the paper read against the appendix, which is the next pass on this source.

Dissected for one structure: the suspensory ligament of the fetlock, which is a short flexor turned to ligament and still carrying striated muscle inside it. Cunningham sectioned it and looked at the sections under a microscope.
Schilling's chondrichthyan, from Kryvi's fibre-type work. Not a holocephalan and not the Squalus of the cranial rows — a third cartilaginous fish, in the corpus for the axial series only.
Ground-dwelling, and the base column in Zaaf et al.

Schreiweis's type species, described in full, with 13 other penguins recorded as differences from it. A wing-propelled diver whose forelimb is a flipper — previously refused as an Aves exemplar, which under species-level scoring is not a judgement the dataset has to make.

Skinks, now largely subsumed into Plestiodon — kept as the name Russell & Bauer's sources use. **Genus-level record**: the sources name the genus and not always a species, so rows land here rather than on a binomial nobody stated.

Cunningham's *Dasypus sexcinctus*. Its interest is that the muscles which have gone are still there as fibrous bands in exactly their own positions — a muscle map drawn in ligament, which he says no author had noticed before.

Bauer (1997), one adult. Its squamosal carries both a lengthened posterior process and a laterally projecting suspensorial crest, which between them embrace the depressor mandibulae origin — the most elaborate skull attachment for that muscle among the salamandrids he examined.

The tetrapodomorph fish of the fins-to-limbs literature. Molnar et al. rate tetrapod-like muscle reconstructions in it 'highly speculative': its deltoideus, pectoralis and forearm masses have correlates, but the individual muscles Andrews & Westoll (1970a) named are not supported as separate muscles.
The dissection-lab carnivoran, and the register most lab handouts are written in.
Bodenham et al.'s second non-crocodyliform crocodylomorph.
Ercoli et al.'s animal; the source of most therian limb rows. A semi-fossorial mustelid, not a generalised mammal.
Abdala & Diogo's avian exemplar, and the bird most often dissected.

McKitrick's described specimen, CM 2320, with a second (USNM 504983) for within-species variation. A foot-propelled diver, so its forelimb is not a generalised flier's — which is the point of having it alongside the crane, the tinamou and the penguin.
Specialised climber. Differs from Eublepharis in which BONE several muscles reach.
Dissected by Walker (1973), Testudinidae. The largest animal in his sample; graviportal.
Fisher & Goodman's complete neognath myology.
Hattori & Tsuihiji's second bird, against Gallus. Not the same animal as Grus americana, which is in this dataset for Fisher & Goodman (1955).

Gila monster and beaded lizard. Heavy-bodied helodermatids, in Russell & Bauer on Shufeldt (1890). **Genus-level record**: the sources name the genus and not always a species, so rows land here rather than on a binomial nobody stated.

Bauer (1997), one adult. A bolitoglossine plethodontid, and the animal in his sample whose depressor mandibulae is divided into two muscles separated along their whole length — the condition of the whole tribe.
Terrestrial.

Wall lizards. Russell & Bauer's most-cited lacertid, largely on Fürbringer and Ribbing. **Genus-level record**: the sources name the genus and not always a species, so rows land here rather than on a binomial nobody stated.

Haas (1973) is the sole reference in his own list for this animal, and it is the lizard he uses to overturn Lakjer on the snake adductor: it has no temporal arch, an elongate temporal region and a widely open braincase, so the muscle layers can be traced in a lizard that is built like a snake.

The smallest of the three, and the one that differs: four palmaris longus tendons where the other two have five, a less proximal abductor digiti I longus origin, and a two-bellied lateral digital extensor where the jaguar has one. Called 'wildcat' throughout the paper, which is not Felis silvestris.

Intermediate in size between the jaguar and Geoffroy's cat, and intermediate in most of Sanchez et al.'s characters — which is why it is worth its own rows rather than being read off either neighbour.
Dissected by Walker (1973), Cheloniidae — **pectoral limb only**. Paired with Caretta so that the two flippers between them cover both limbs.
Naumann et al.'s animal. A non-teleost actinopterygian, which is the point: its cucullaris development is evidence about the branchiomeric condition, not about teleosts.
Cunningham's *Lutra vulgaris*. Its five webbed digits still move freely, and he says the foot meets the requirements of his three-layer type more nearly than any other carnivore he dissected.

Haas (1973) dissected a very large specimen in the Field Museum, Chicago, and describes it as his own. Genus only — he does not name the species. The animal matters because its venom gland is enclosed in an uninterrupted muscular loop, which is what shows the compressor glandulae to be a single adductor mandibulae externus superficialis.

Cunningham's *Meles taxus*, and his test of whether a plantigrade foot behaves differently from a digitigrade one. His answer is that it does not: the intrinsic muscles are as plantar in position in the badger as in the digitigrade carnivores.
Schilling's mammal for perivertebral fibre types, sectioned between the 6th and 7th lumbar vertebrae — the animal behind the claim that the transversospinal muscle subdivides in mammals.
Marsupial, against the placental exemplars.

**A partial dissection, and Cunningham says why**: the animal was so putrid that the deeper layers could not be opened. He records the adducting muscles and nothing else, so this species carries one row here and should carry no more from this source.
Schilling's agnathan. The perivertebral cross-section in his Fig. 2 is this animal, which is why the axial rows that cited him for a lamprey now sit here.
The commonest teaching salamander, and aquatic in Omura et al.'s series.
Palaeognath, in Widrig et al.'s 3D atlas.
Bauer (1997), one adult. Deeper fibres of its depressor mandibulae attach to a sesamoid that presumably develops inside the muscle's own tendon.

Cunningham's *Trichechus rosmarus* — a very young specimen long preserved in spirit in Edinburgh. He disagrees with Murie's account of its pedal muscles at three points and says which, so the rows carry both readings.

Glass lizards. Limbless anguids, on Humphry (1872a) — the limb muscles are what remains after limb loss. **Genus-level record**: the sources name the genus and not always a species, so rows land here rather than on a binomial nobody stated.

Gambaryan et al.'s platypus is a single juvenile retaining its teeth, so nothing here is checked against adult variation. It is the more primitive of the monotremes BELOW the elbow and the more derived above it, which is why the genus cannot stand in for the clade in either direction.

Early Carboniferous whatcheeriid, and the reason the stem-tetrapod column can be scored at all. Bishop (2014) documented scarring fine enough to resolve what may be individual muscle fascicles, which let him reconstruct the forelimb without strict bracketing — Molnar & Diogo call it a Lagerstätte-like bracket taxon. Molnar et al. rate its reconstruction 'supported by both fossil and comparative data', against 'highly speculative' for the tetrapodomorph fish.

The third term of the series, and the end of it: the sheep's suspensory ligament has no muscular tissue left at all, only rings of fat cells with vessels and nerves among them where the muscle used to be.

Dissected alongside Crocodylus porosus by Hattori & Tsuihiji, who report no difference between them in any pedal muscle. Their crocodylian accounts are therefore two animals, not one, and both carry rows.

One of Cunningham's four tetradactylous cats. Its abductor minimi digiti is caught mid-fusion: coalesced with the abductor of the metatarsal for an inch at the origin, then running as a flat tendon incorporated into the surface of the short flexor before separating again at the toe.

The largest of Sanchez et al.'s three South American felids and the most fully described. Its forearm differs from the smaller two in bulk more than in arrangement: supinator, pronators and brachioradialis all better developed, and its flexor digitorum profundus carries two sesamoid bones.

Cunningham's *Felis leopardus*, from the Edinburgh anatomical museum. **The best-developed abducting apparatus of the little toe among the tetradactylous carnivores he examined** — three separate slips where the dog has none.
The procellariiform McKitrick dissected against the loons to test a proposed loon-tubenose relationship, which her characters do not support. Here for one sourced absence, the supinator.
Common spadefoot toad. One of Prikryl et al.'s (2009) nine frogs. A burrower, and the only one of them in which the pyriformis was absent from every specimen.
Dissected by Walker (1973), Pelomedusidae. One of his two pleurodires — the side-necked lineage, and the outgroup to every cryptodire statement in the dataset.

A single specimen, and the smallest of Cunningham's three — the hand is one inch long, so the intrinsic muscles are described from one dissection rather than the four he had of the thylacine manus. **Fore limb only.** The pelvis and hind limbs were destroyed by shot before he received them, so this animal is absent from every hindlimb record on purpose.
A walking frog rather than a jumper. Formerly Kassina maculata.

Horned lizards. Dorsoventrally flattened phrynosomatids; Jenkins & Tanner found three bellies where others found one. **Genus-level record**: the sources name the genus and not always a species, so rows land here rather than on a binomial nobody stated.

Surinam toad, an obligate aquatic pipid. One of Prikryl et al.'s (2009) nine frogs and the most derived: its iliac shaft is twisted so that the originally inner surface faces dorsally, and it has a pulmonum proprius running from the lungs to the femur.
Skinks. Scincid with a reduced limb, on Nash & Tanner (1970). **Genus-level record**: the sources name the genus and not always a species, so rows land here rather than on a binomial nobody stated.
Arboreal procyonid; the second caniform against Galictis.

Cunningham's *Hyrax capensis*, one of the six feet the Challenger Commission gave him. He is checking Murie & Mivart, who had described the same muscles as 'single and double interossei' without classifying them.

Described in 2012 and hypothesised to be the sister group of all other eels, living and fossil, on more plesiomorphic osteology than any other eel and on mitogenomic data. Springer & Johnson's material is USNM 396051, 156 mm TL, with a second specimen at 73.8 mm. Not a proxy for teleosts: it is a specialised deep-reef eel whose interest here is that it retains characters other eels have lost.

Cunningham names no species. **His most complete intermediate layer**: a two-headed short flexor for every digit, all eight slips separate along their whole length and lying in one plane, with no dorsal interossei at all.

Cunningham's *Felis concolor*, one of the six feet the Challenger Commission supplied him for the pes survey. Its abducting apparatus for the little toe is the leopard's minus the supernumerary third slip.

Edible frog. The standard model of anuran musculoskeletal anatomy (Gaupp 1896; Dunlap 1960) — and for that reason NOT the baseline Prikryl et al. (2009) chose: they call it highly derived and describe Discoglossus pictus instead, because discoglossoid skeletal features are known from the Middle Jurassic. Useful precisely as the derived comparison.
The dissection-lab rodent.
Abdala & Diogo's anuran exemplar.

Huber et al.'s (2011) batoid exemplar, described alongside *Squalus acanthias* and *Hydrolagus colliei* in the same chapter, each with its own table of origins and insertions. The reading note called it *Rhinoptera percellens* until 2026-08-20 — the wrong genus, *Rhinoptera* being the cownose rays; Huber et al. write *Rhinobatos* throughout.

Bauer (1997), larval and adult. The one salamandrid he examined in which the gonial does not fuse with the articular (Francis 1934), so its depressor mandibulae insertion can be scored on the gonial alone.

Spiny lizards. Phrynosomatid, and the animal behind Reilly's electromyography that Dick & Clemente's Table 1 draws on. **Genus-level record**: the sources name the genus and not always a species, so rows land here rather than on a binomial nobody stated.

Stout sawpalate, a bathypelagic serrivomerid. Its gill-arch musculature had never been described or illustrated before Springer & Johnson (2015), and its epibranchials completely lack gill filaments — a condition those authors report from nowhere else.

Snubnosed or pug-nosed eel, which burrows into the flesh of larger fish. Springer & Johnson (2015) describe both dorsal and ventral gill-arch series in full. All three obliqui ventrales are absent, which they associate with its exceptionally heavy ventral musculature.

Cunningham's 'Cuscus (Phalangista maculata)', a single specimen, and his arboreal counterweight to the thylacine: clavicle complete, subclavius ordinary, a long coraco-brachialis reaching the supracondyloid foramen, and a plantar cartilage in the sole instead of a heel. Where the thylacine and the phascogale disagree, the cuscus usually tells you which difference is about locomotion.
The classroom shark, and the exemplar behind most chondrichthyan rows here.
Palaeognath; the source of the avian architecture data.

Kaup's arrowtooth eel, a deep-sea synaphobranchid. Springer & Johnson (2015) describe its ventral gill-arch muscles first-hand; its sphincter pharyngis is so dominant that the recti cannot be read separately from it.

Cunningham's *Myrmecophaga tamandua*. **Its adductors work towards the annularis and its abductors away from the index** — the two halves of the intrinsic apparatus referred to different digits, which he says is unique so far as he knows, and which leaves the index with four intrinsic muscles.
Wall geckos. Gekkotan. **Genus-level record**: the sources name the genus and not always a species, so rows land here rather than on a binomial nobody stated.
Bauer (1997), one adult plus one metamorphosing specimen. Its depressor mandibulae had never been described before.
Walthall & Ashley-Ross's animal, and the source of most Caudata attachment rows.

Late Triassic basal theropod from the Hayden Quarry, Ghost Ranch, New Mexico. Burch (2014) reconstructs its complete forelimb myology from multiple well-preserved individuals — the completeness is why it, rather than a better-known theropod, is the exemplar here.
Winterbottom's descriptive synonymy is a survey of teleost muscle names rather than one dissection; rows citing it are a generalisation, not a specimen.

Werneburg's Appendix 1 is a catalogue of 94 turtle cranial muscular units compiled across the literature back to Bojanus (1819-21), not a description of one animal: 30 of its 73 two-ended entries give the origin or insertion as a range across turtles ('or', '1-2 heads', 'the possible second head'). Rows citing it are a clade generalisation, not a specimen.
Dissected by Walker (1973), Testudinidae. A terrestrial tortoise against his aquatic emydid type.

Cunningham's principal animal, and the one he had two of. Extinct since 1936, so the myology cannot be redone — these rows are from a dissection of a Challenger specimen and there will not be another. Its clavicle is a vestige embedded in the cephalo-humeral muscle with no attachment to the acromion, which reorganises the whole shoulder relative to the two other marsupials here; Cunningham reads the resemblance to the placental carnivores as convergence and is careful to say which muscles carry it.

Elpistostegalian, and the node at which the latissimus dorsi process appears. Its girdle is nearly mute on muscle: Molnar et al. report only faint rugosities above the glenoid and a hollow above the coracoid foramen.
Abdala & Diogo's lepidosaur exemplar.
Abdala & Diogo's chelonian exemplar.

Cunningham's 'Phalangista vulpina' — the Challenger's four specimens, used as a check on the cuscus rather than described in its own right. Its hand resembles the cuscus's closely, with the adductor group feebler and the median raphe correspondingly less distinct.
Meller's chameleon. Molnar et al. (2017) dissected one wild-caught subadult, both sides — the second of their two chameleons, and the larger at 27 cm SVL.
Dissected by Walker (1973), Trionychidae. A softshell, and the family in which the deltoid complex does not spread onto the scapular prong at all.
Blotto et al.'s standard reference for the four layers of hand and foot musculature.

Bauer (1997), larval and adult, but only the larva is described in his Results; his adult Triturus material is T. karelini, T. helveticus, T. marmoratus and T. vulgaris. The binomial follows the source, which uses T. cristatus s.str. after karelini was raised to species rank.
Bauer (1997), one adult; its depressor mandibulae had never been described before. Now usually placed in Lissotriton; the binomial follows the source.
Bauer (1997), one adult; its depressor mandibulae had never been described before. Elevated from a subspecies of T. cristatus only in the 1980s, which is why the older literature has nothing on it.
Bauer (1997), one adult. The only Triturus he examined whose depressor mandibulae inserts through a single short tendon carrying all the muscle's fibres.
Bauer (1997), larval and adult. Now usually placed in Lissotriton; the binomial follows the source.

Tegus. Large-bodied teiids, in Russell & Bauer largely on Fisher & Tanner. **Genus-level record**: the sources name the genus and not always a species, so rows land here rather than on a binomial nobody stated.
Cervical musculature at vertebra-by-vertebra resolution.

Leaf-tailed geckos. Arboreal gekkotan whose serratus origin extends onto the anterior thoracic ribs. **Genus-level record**: the sources name the genus and not always a species, so rows land here rather than on a binomial nobody stated.

Dick & Clemente's Table 1 gives origin and insertion 'of the varanid hindlimb' as a compilation from Snyder (1954), Gans et al., Reilly on Sceloporus clarki and Anzai et al. on Cuban Anolis — two of the four not varanids — with no per-muscle provenance to trace back. The architecture in that paper is their own measurement across 9 varanid species and 27 individuals; the attachments are inherited and belong to no one animal.

Hattori & Tsuihiji's second squamate, against Iguana. The two differ in the pedal muscles more than the paper's clade-level headings suggest — the monitor has two extra short-extensor slips to digits I and II, and a tibialis anterior origin that runs to the distal end of the tibia where the iguana's does not.

Haas (1973) lists himself alongside Lightoller (1939) and Frazzetta (1962) for this animal and says his account is based on all those sources together — so rows citing him here are a synthesis, not a single dissection, and say so.
Night lizards. Xantusiid. **Genus-level record**: the sources name the genus and not always a species, so rows land here rather than on a binomial nobody stated.

Gambaryan et al.'s primary subject and the first comparative myology of the genus since Allen (1912): three specimens against two echidnas and one platypus. Its individual variation is concentrated below the elbow and is driven by reduction of the marginal fingers, so the authors recommend Z. bartoni — which keeps all five claws — as the better model. That animal has not been dissected.
